content.text:
For a **typical cold**, there’s no medicine that “cures” it—most colds improve on their own in about **7–10 days**. Medicines can help you feel better while your body clears the virus. ([mayoclinic.org](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/common-cold/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20351611?sf237848573=1&utm_source=openai))

**Common options for adults:**

- **Fever, headache, body aches, sore throat:**  
  **Acetaminophen** or **ibuprofen** can help. Follow the label, and avoid doubling up—many “multi-symptom” cold products already contain acetaminophen. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))

- **Stuffy nose:**  
  **Saline nasal spray/rinse** is safe for most people. A decongestant such as **pseudoephedrine** may help, but ask a pharmacist/clinician first if you have **high blood pressure, heart disease, thyroid disease, glaucoma, prostate/urination problems**, or take certain antidepressants.

- **Cough:**  
  **Honey** can soothe cough in adults and children over 1 year old. Some people use **dextromethorphan** for a dry cough or **guaifenesin** for mucus, but benefits can be modest.

- **Runny nose/sneezing:**  
  An antihistamine may help, but some cause sleepiness and dry mouth.

**Avoid antibiotics** unless a clinician says you have a bacterial infection—colds are viral.

**Important for children:** OTC cough/cold medicines are **not recommended for children under 6** by CDC guidance; FDA specifically warns not to give OTC cough/cold products to children **under 2**, and many labels say not under 4. For young kids, ask a pediatrician/pharmacist. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))

**See a doctor or urgent care** if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, dehydration, confusion, symptoms that worsen after improving, fever lasting more than 3 days, or symptoms lasting more than 10 days. Also consider testing for **COVID/flu** if you have fever, body aches, significant fatigue, or known exposure.
